Reasonable
REE-zn-a-bl
adj. (rational; belonging to the mind; fitting to reason)
Greek logikos, of or belonging to logos — reason, word. The Authorized Version renders it reasonable at Romans 12:1 and of the word at 1 Peter 2:2. The English word has drifted toward moderate; the Greek means rational, belonging to a mind, as against merely bodily or ceremonial.

Biblical Definition

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. The word does not mean moderate, and Paul is not asking for a measured, sensible, proportionate religion. Logikos means rational — the worship of a creature who has a mind and knows why he is doing it. Under the old covenant a man brought a beast that had no idea what was happening to it. Paul says the Christian brings himself, knowingly, understanding the mercies by which he is asked. That is the force of therefore: eleven chapters of doctrine stand behind the appeal, and the appeal is addressed to men who have followed the argument. Two things follow. First, this worship is embodied — your bodies, not your sentiments; the sacrifice is living and walks about. Second, it is intelligent, and therefore inseparable from the renewing of the mind that Paul immediately commands. Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. A worship that bypasses the understanding is not the reasonable service of Romans 12, whatever its intensity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): having the faculty of reason; governed by reason; conformable to reason; just; rational.

expand to see more

REASONABLE, a. Having the faculty of reason; endued with reason; as a reasonable being.

REASONABLE, a. Governed by reason; being under the influence of reason; thinking, speaking or acting rationally or according to the dictates of reason.

REASONABLE, a. Conformable or agreeable to reason; just; rational.

SERVICE, n. The act of serving; that which is done in obedience to a superior; also, public worship or religious duties performed.

SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God; anything consecrated and offered to God or to a divinity.

Key Scripture

Romans 12:1 — "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service."

Romans 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

1 Corinthians 6:20 — "For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's."

Psalm 51:17 — "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."

Modern Corruption

The English drift from rational to moderate has been read back into Romans 12:1, producing a religion of reasonable proportions; and the opposite error strips worship of the understanding altogether.

expand to see more

Because reasonable now means moderate in ordinary English, Romans 12:1 is quoted for a temperate, balanced discipleship that does not go to extremes. The text says the opposite. The sacrifice is the whole body, presented once and for all, and there is nothing moderate about a burnt offering. What is reasonable about it is that the man understands what he is doing and why — by the mercies of God. Read rightly, the verse forbids exactly the half-measure it is usually quoted to defend.

The contrary corruption is older and more common in the churches: worship that aims at the affections by going around the understanding. The regulative principle stands against it, and so does this word. Where the mind is bypassed — by spectacle, by volume, by manufactured atmosphere, by a liturgy in a tongue the people do not know — the offering may be sincere but it is not logikos. Paul ties the living sacrifice to the renewed mind in the very next sentence, and the two cannot be separated without loss.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logikos (G3050), rational, belonging to the word or reason; paristemi (G3936), to present or offer; thusia (G2378), sacrifice; metamorphoo (G3339), to be transformed.

expand to see more

Greek logikos (G3050) — rational, pertaining to reason; rendered reasonable here and of the word at 1 Peter 2:2, its only two occurrences.

Greek paristemi (G3936) — to place beside, to present; the technical word for presenting an offering at the altar.

Greek thusia (G2378) — a sacrifice, the thing offered; here qualified as living, against every slain beast before it.

Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to be transformed, changed in form; the same word used of the transfiguration.

Greek anakainosis (G342) — renewing, a making new; of the mind, not the feelings.

Usage

"“which is your reasonable service” — worship offered by a creature who understands."

"“present your bodies a living sacrifice” — embodied, not merely inward."

"“by the mercies of God” — the ground of the appeal, and what makes it reasonable."
